title: Motia Khanna vs Lalit Sharma on 29 August, 2024
full_text: Motia Khanna vs Lalit Sharma on 29 August, 2024 IN THE COURT OF SH. MAYANK AGGARWAL, JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE FIRST CLASS-01, N.I. ACT, SOUTH DISTRICT, SAKET COURTS, DELHI CT Case no. 49/2018 PS Safdarjung Enclave u/s 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 Motia Khanna vs Lalit Sharma JUDGMENT A. S.NO. OF THE CASE : 49/2018 B. DATE OF INSTITUTION : 03.02.2018 C. DATE OF OFFENCE : After 15th day of service of legal demand notice issued by complainant D. NAME OF THE : Ms. Motia Khanna COMPLAINANT W/oRameshChanderSharma R/o DG 99, Sarojini Nagar, Delhi. E. NAME OF THE ACCUSED : Sh. Lalit Sharma S/o Late Sh. S.B Sharma R/o40-1/2YusufSarai Village, Delhi. F. OFFENCE : u/s 138 NI Act COMPLAINED OF G. PLEA OF ACCUSED : Pleaded not guilty H. FINAL ORDER : CONVICTION I. DATE OF FINAL ORDER : 29.08.2024 CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 1 of 21 BRIEF FACTS: 1. The present case has been initiated at the instance of Ms. Motia Khanna (hereinafter referred to as the Complainant) against Sh. Lalit Sharma (hereinafter referred to as the Accused) u/s 138 of the Negotiable Instrument Act (hereinafter referred to as the NI Act ) in relation to dishonor of cheque bearing number no 121262, dated 25.01.2017 drawn on Central Bank of India, Green Park, Delhi, for an amount of Rs. 5,00,000 (Rs. Five Lakhs only) (hereinafter referred to as the cheque in question) allegedly issued for discharge of the liability towards the complainant by the accused. 2. Briefly stated, it is the case of the complainant that the complainant was the owner of vehicle (Car, make Vento, white colour) bearing no DL10CC 1645 and the same was financed with ICICI Bank for five years for an EMI of Rs.16,785 (total 60 EMIs). That one Sh. Dinesh Gautam approached the complainant for purchasing the aforesaid vehicle and accordingly vide agreement dated 04.07.2015, the said vehicle was sold to Sh. Dinesh Gautam by the complainant for a total consideration of Rs. 4,00,000 and the possession was also handed over to Sh. Dinesh Gautam. That as per the agreement it was agreed between the parties that Sh. Dinesh Gautam shall be paying the balance 24 installments of Rs. 16,785 in respect of the said vehicle and accordingly the sale consideration was fixed for Rs. 4,00,000. It is further alleged that since Sh. Dinesh Gautam paid only three EMIs after the purchase, the remaining EMIs (in total Rs.3,52,485) were deducted from the account of CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 2 of 21 the Complainant and were never paid by Sh. Dinesh Gautam. Consequently, a complaint was filed with PS Safdarjung Enclave by the complainant and in order to put the dispute at rest, the accused, being the maternal uncle of Sh. Dinesh Gautam, issued the cheque in question to the complainant. It is further alleged that cheque in question for Rs.5,00,000 was issued to the complainant by the accused for payment of the due amount and including compensation for the metal agony and harassment caused to the complainant for a period of over two years. Lastly, it is alleged that upon presentation, the said cheque got dishonored vide memo dated 26.01.2017, for the reason "Funds Insufficient" and consequently a legal demand notice was sent demanding the amount of cheque on 25.11.2017, however, despite the same, payment was not made by the accused. 3. Accordingly, complaint was filed u/s 138 NI Act by the complainant and upon consideration of the same cognizance was taken and summons were issued qua the accused vide order dated 03.02.2018. Thereafter, on 17.01.2019, notice was framed against the accused upon which the accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Further a defence was taken by the accused that the accused never had any transaction with the complainant. That the cheque in question was given by the accused to Sh. Kamal Motwani, son-in law of the complainant, for getting the loan of the accused transferred from Central Bank to some NBFC. That he also paid a cash amount of Rs. 3,50,000 to Sh. Kamal Motwani, however the loan was not CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 3 of 21 transferred and the cheque in question has been misused by the Complainant. Lastly, the accused admitted his signature on the cheque in question but denied having received the legal demand notice. EVIDENCE LED BY THE PARTIES 4. The Complainant examined herself as CW1 in order to prove her case. In her examination in chief, she relied upon and tendered her evidence by way of affidavit Ex. CW1/A and relied upon the following documents:- i. Mark CW1/A, copy of agreement dated 04.07.2015 to sale of the vehicle ii. MarkCW1/2, copy of police complaint dated 26.04.2017 iii. Ex.CW1/3, certified copy of the bank account of complainant. iv. Ex.CW1/4, NOC dated 08.05.2017 v. Ex.CW1/5, cheque in question vi Ex.CW1/6, cheque return memo vii Ex. CW1/7, legal demand notice viii Ex.CW1/8, postal receipts ix Ex.CW1/9, tracking report x Ex. CW1/10, complaint. 5. Further, CW-1 was cross-examined by Ld. Counsel for the accused on 18.04.2023. Thereafter, on 30.11.2023, statement of accused u/s 313 Cr.P.C. was recorded wherein the accused stated that he does not know anything about the transaction in CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 4 of 21 question. That he has not given any cheque to the complainant. That the accused was in talks of obtaining a loan of Rs.10,00,000 from the husband of the complainant, namely, Sh. Ramesh Khanna and even received Rs. 5,00,000 from the said Sh. Ramesh Khanna. That the accused had given two signed blank cheques to the husband of the complainant as security in lieu of the loan. That the cheque in question has been misused by the complainant and her husband. Lastly, it was stated that he did not received the legal demand notice and the notice bears incorrect address. 6. Subsequently, in his defence, accused examined Sh. Dinesh Gautam as DW1. He deposed that, complainant's son in law Kamal Motwani, sold the car of the complainant to him and an agreement was executed between him and the complainant. That he made payment of certain EMIs and asked Mr. Motwani to transfer the car in his name, however the transfer was not done. It was further deposed that the possession of the car from him was taken in July 2016. It was also deposed that Sh. Motwani, took 4-5 cheques from him in respect of the said transaction and also filed one case for dishonour of cheque against him. Lastly, he admitted that the accused is his uncle. ARGUMENTS ADVANCED BY PARTIES 7. Final arguments were heard on behalf of both the parties at length. CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 5 of 21 8. Ld. Counsel for the complainant argued that the complainant received the cheque in question from the accused against settlement of the dispute between the complainant and the nephew of the accused (DW1). It was further argued that the transaction of sale of the car of the complainant stands admitted on the part of DW1(nephew of the accused) and also the factum of possession of car having been handed over to DW1. It was further argued that the accused has admitted his signature on the cheque in question (Ex.CW1/5) and accordingly mandatory presumption gets raised in favour of the complainant and the accused has failed to rebut the same. It is further argued that as per sec 138 NI Act , it is not required that the cheque in question must be issued by the accused for discharge of his own liability towards the complainant and thus the fact that the accused never had any transaction with the complainant is inconsequential. 9. It is further argued by the Ld. Counsel that despite thorough cross examination of the complainant the accused has failed to impeach the credibility of the complainant. It is further argued that the accused has failed to show on record that the demand notice was issued by the complainant at the wrong address and therefore due service of the notice has to be presumed. Lastly, it is argued that the fact that the accused has taken contradictory stands as regards the issuance and custody of the cheque in question at different stages of the trial further weakens the defence taken by the accused and lends credibility to the case of the complainant. Accordingly, Ld. Counsel for complainant CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 6 of 21 argued that the accused must be convicted in the present case for the offence punishable u/s 138 of NI Act. 10. Per contra, it was argued by the Ld. Counsel on behalf of the accused that the accused has never done any transaction with the complainant and as such there is no legally enforceable liability of the accused towards the complainant. It was further argued that the legal demand notice has been issued by the complainant at the wrong address of the accused and accordingly, the offence u/s 138 NI Act is not made out. It is further argued that the accused never issued the cheque in question to the complainant and the same has been misused by the complainant. It is further argued that the particulars on the cheque in question are not filled by the accused. Accordingly, it is argued that the accused must be acquitted as accused has successfully rebutted the presumption available to the complainant. APPRAISAL 11. Before appreciating the facts of the case in detail for the purpose of decision, let relevant position of law be discussed. Section 138 of the Act provides as under: Section 138 .- Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account.- Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 7 of 21 whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless-- (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation -- for the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability. CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 8 of 21 12. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under S.138 N.I. Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: (A) drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, for payment to another person from out of that account for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; (B) cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier; (C) returning the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque, (D) giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount, (E) failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 9 of 21 Therefore, it is only when all the aforementioned ingredients are satisfied that the person who had drawn the cheque can be deemed to have committed an offence under Section 138 of the N I Act. 13. The Act further raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque i.e., complainant in the present case; firstly, in regard to the passing of consideration as contained in Section 118 (a) therein and, secondly, a presumption under Section 139 , that the holder of cheque receiving the same of the nature referred to in Section 138 for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 14. Analyzing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa , AIR 2019 SC 1983, noted as follows: (i) Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. (ii) The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 10 of 21 (iii) To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. (iv) That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence, Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. (v) It is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box to support his defence. 15. To put in nutshell, the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 of the Act, the presumptions under Sections 118 (a) and 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as execution of cheque by accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, that the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The onus to prove the issuance of the cheque lies upon the complainant, and the same has to be proved beyond reasonable doubt, unless the accused admits the same. Once the issuance of cheque is established, either by CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 11 of 21 admission or by positive evidence, the presumption under Section 139 of the Act comes into play. 16. As per s. 139 of the Act it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in Section 138 , for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. Therefore, here the onus shifts upon the accused to prove the non-existence of debt or other liability. Section 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 uses the word "shall presume", which means that the presumption under Section 139 is rebuttable. The standard of proof required to rebut the presumption under Section 139 is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or other liability, the onus shifts back to the complainant to prove by way of evidence, beyond reasonable doubt, that the cheque in question was issued by the accused in discharge, whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. If the accused is able to raise a probable defence, then the presumptions under Section 118 (a) and Section 139 will not come to the aid of the complainant. For this purpose, the accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the cheque in question was not supported by consideration, and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. 17. At the same time, it is clear that a bare denial of passing of consideration and existence of debt, apparently would not serve CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 12 of 21 the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances upon the consideration of which, the Court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist, or their non-existence was so probable that a prudent man would, under circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist. From the legal provisions and the law laid down in various judgments, it can be safely gathered that it is for the accused to rebut the presumptions. He can do so by cross examining the complainant, or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. It is amply clear that the accused does not need to discharge his or her liability beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt. He just needs to create holes in the case set out by the complainant and create a reasonable doubt over the version put forth by the complainant. 18. Reverting to the facts of the case at hand, it is the case of the complainant that accused had issued the cheque in question for settlement of the dispute between the complainant and the nephew (DW1) of the accused in respect of a transaction for sale of the car of the complainant which included the compensation amount for the harassment caused to the complainant on account of non-payment by DW1, which got dishonored upon presentation. It is further alleged by the complainant that despite issuance of legal notice ie. Ex.CW1/7, CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 13 of 21 accused neither issued any response nor made the payment of the cheque amount. 19. On the other hand, the accused has admitted his signatures on the cheque in question at all the stages of trial, however disputed the fact of filling the other particulars of the cheque and he has also taken different stand as regards the purpose of issuance and custody of the cheque in question. Now, in view of the admission of execution of the cheque in question by the accused, statutory presumption u/s 139 of the NI Act is liable to the attracted in favour of the complainant. Further, since the accused has admitted his signatures on the cheque, in light of sec 20 of the NI Act , filling of the particulars of the cheque by the complainant is not barred. 20. In " Bir Singh vs Mukesh Kumar , (2019) 4 SCC 197" it has been held that; a meaningful reading of the provisions of the NI Act including, in particular, Sections 20 , 87 and 139 , makes it amply clear that a person who signs a cheque and makes it over to the payee remains liable unless he adduces evidence to rebut the presumption that the cheque had been issued for payment of a debt or in discharge of a liability. It is immaterial that the cheque may have been filled in by any person other than the drawer, if the cheque is duly signed by the drawer. If a signed blank cheque is voluntarily presented to a payee, towards some payment, the payee may fill up the amount and other particular and it has to be ascertained whether such presumption of legal liability or debt in favour of the complainant was rebutted by CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 14 of 21 the accused during the trial or not. Thus, unless in the ultimate analysis of the matter the accused successfully rebuts the presumption raised in favour of the complainant, the said defence of the accused is liable to be rejected. 21. Another defence taken by the accused during the course of the trial is that there was never any transaction between the accused and the complainant and as such there is no legally enforceable debt or liability in respect of the accused. In respect of the argument raised by the Ld. Counsel for the accused, it is sufficient to state that the argument raised is completely misconceived and in contravention of the mandate of the law. 22. A bare perusal of sec 138 NI Act would clearly reveal that there is no requirement for prosecution u/s 138 NI Act that the drawer of the cheque in question must issue the same for discharge of his own debt. As per the settled position of law, a cheque issued by person A from his own bank account for the discharge of loan due from person B, upon dishonour will make A liable for prosecution u/s 138 NI Act and not B. Thus, even though admittedly there was no transaction between the complainant and the accused, since the cheque in question was issued by the accused for the discharge of liability of his nephew (DW1), the accused is liable to be prosecuted. At this stage, it is further pertinent to state that DW1 in his deposition has expressly admitted not only the fact of entering into a transaction of sale-purchase of car of the complainant and executing an agreement in that respect, the said DW1 has also CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 15 of 21 admitted the factum of payment of only a few EMI's and not all and further the factum of getting the possession of the car upon execution of the agreement. Thus, it is reasonable to state, that the case of the complainant already stands substantially admitted from the evidence brought on behalf of the accused himself. 23. Another defence taken by accused during the course of the trial is that the legal demand notice send by the complainant was sent at the wrong address of the accused. It was argued by the ld. Counsel that since the address on which the legal demand notice was sent was incorrect, the presumption of service cannot be raised in favour of the complainant. To buttress his argument the Ld. Counsel has relied upon judgment titled " R.L Verma and Sons (HUF) vs P C Sharma , AIR Online 2019 DEL 940, Hon'ble Delhi High Court. Now, in this regard it is pertinent to mention that the said defence was taken by the accused only at a later stage of the trial as at the stage of framing of notice, the accused simply denied the fact of having received the notice and did not raised the issue of notice bearing the wrong address. Thus, the said defence primarily seems to be an afterthought. 24. Further, perusal of the record reveals that though the accused has disputed the address on which the demand notice (Ex.CW1/7) was sent by the complainant, however the accused nowhere during the course of the trial brought any material to show the correct address of the accused or the fact that at the CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 16 of 21 relevant point of time the accused was residing at some other place or the fact that the complainant was aware that the address mentioned on the demand notice is incorrect. In fact, DW1 also never disputed the said fact despite being the resident at the same address. Further, during the cross examination of CW1, it was deposed by CW1 that she came to know about the address of the accused from her husband and son in law. Now, in this regard it is pertinent to state that firstly, the accused has nowhere disputed that the husband or the son in law of the complainant were not aware about the address of the accused. Secondly, the accused himself during the course of the trial has taken a defence, though contradictory, that he issued the cheque in question in relation to certain transactions entered into with the husband and son in law of the complainant. Meaning thereby that son in law and the husband of the complainant were indeed known to the accused and thus could be well aware of the address of the accused. Thus, mere denial by the accused that the notice was not sent at the correct address does not relieve the accused from the burden of proving his defence. 25. Further, in the judgment relied upon the Ld. Counsel for the accused, the accused/petitioner was able to bring material to show that the address on which the legal demand notice was sent was incorrect and moreover the complainant was also aware of the correct address of the accused and thus Hon'ble High Court observed that where it is shown that the notice bears incorrect address, presumption of service will not be raised. However, in the present case, the accused has failed to CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 17 of 21 bring any such material on record. Thus, in the absence of any evidence on the part of the accused to show that the address borne by the notice was incorrect and in the light of the foregoing discussion, it is reasonable to observe that the legal demand notice was indeed issued at the correct address of the accused. Further, in the landmark judgment passed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in matter of " C. C. Alavi Haji Vs. Palapetty Mohd. & Anr. " reported in {(2007) 6 Supreme Court Cases 555}, it has been held that :- " A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court alongwith the copy of complaint Under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required Under Section 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary Under Section 27 of G. C. Act and 114 of the Evidence Act ". 26. So, in light of above said judgment and discussion, this Court is of the opinion that defence of accused, that the notice was sent at the wrong address and thus not received by him is without any force and is hereby rejected. 27. Further, during the course of the trial the accused has taken different stand as regards the transaction in respect of which the cheque in question was allegedly issued and to whom it was issued. On one hand, the accused has taken a defence that he was transacting with the son in law of the complainant Sh. CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 18 of 21 Kamal Motwani for getting his loan account transferred to some NBFC and the cheque in question were issued to Sh. Kamal Motwani in respect of the said transaction, whereas on the other hand the accused took a stand that the cheque in question was issued as a security cheque to the husband of the complainant for obtaining a loan of Rs. 10,00,000, out of which Rs. 5,00,000 were in fact received by him. Needless to state, that the accused has not brought any evidence on record to substantiate the said claim(s). Moreover, taking contradictory stands at different stages of the trial further weakens the case of the accused. Accused was required to prove non existence of liability/ debt by either direct evidence or by bringing on record his defence, on a scale of preponderance of probabilities, but he has failed to do so. Further, as already stated before, DW1 has substantially admitted all the key elements/allegations of the case of the complainant which fact further lends credit to the case of the complainant. Lastly, despite thorough cross examination of the complainant (CW1), the accused has failed to impeach the credibility of the witness or to bring any material contradictions on record. 28. As per settled position of law, it is only when the accused is able to raise a probable defence regarding the non-existence of the liability that the onus shifts upon the complainant to prove its case. However, upon considering the record, this court is of the opinion that accused has not been able to create any credible doubt in respect of the case of the complainant and accused has not been able to raise a "probable defence" in his CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 19 of 21 favour. The accused did not lead any cogent evidence to rebut the presumption of law in favour of the complainant and he has failed to point out the fallacies in the case set up by the complainant in order to rebut the presumption on a scale of preponderance of probabilities. As already observed by the Hon'ble Apex Court, mere denial on the part of the accused is not sufficient to rebut the presumption existing in favour of the complainant. CONCLUSION 29. In view of the provision of section 139 of the Act r/w Section 118 of the Act, the Court has to presume that cheque has been issued for discharging debt or liability. The said presumption which is rebuttable could be rebutted by accused by proving the contrary. For shifting the burden, accused had to prove his defence by preponderance of probabilities, whereas, in the present case, the accused has completely failed to do so. Infact the case of the complainant stands substantially admitted from the record. As such, upon comprehensive perusal of the evidence led on record it appears that the accused has failed to rebut the presumption in favour of the complainant and has failed to create any doubt over the case put forth by the complainant. 30. Though the accused is not required to conclusively prove his evidence in support of his defence to rebut the presumption but he has to show certain circumstances or lead evidence so that the court either believes his defence to exist or the court CT No. 49/2018 u/s 138 NI Act, Motia Khanna Vs. Lalit Sharma Page no. 20 of 21 considers its existence so probable that a prudent man would, under the circumstances of the case, believe the same. However, in the present case, the accused has failed to meet the required threshold. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. Without rebutting the presumption, the onus to prove his case will not shift to complainant. It is clear the accused has not led any cogent evidence to rebut presumptions under S. 118 / 139 of the Act. ORDER 31. Accordingly, for the reasons stated above, this court hereby Convicts the accused Lalit Sharma for the offence punishable u/s 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 in respect of cheque in question. 32. Copy of this judgment be given free of cost to the accused against receiving. ANNOUNCED IN OPEN COURT Today i.e. 29.08.2024 (Mayank Aggarwal) Judicial Magistrate First Class-01 N.I.
